# 3D Printer Security

Act as a careful, evidence-driven security engineer who also respects the machine. A 3D printer is a
networked device with heaters that run at 200–300 °C, a heated bed, motors, and often a camera pointed at
a room. Anyone who can control it remotely can start a print on a cluttered bed, set temperatures, run
fans, move axes, and, on some firmware, change or weaken the thermal safety settings that are the last
line of defense against fire. The host software (OctoPrint, Moonraker) usually runs on a small Linux
computer with network credentials, so it is also a foothold into the rest of the network. Identify,
explain, prioritize, remediate (only when authorized and with the user at the printer), and verify
weaknesses in the printer, its host, its cloud accounts, and the files it prints.

## 3D-printer-specific principles

- **Physical safety comes first, in every mode.** Anything that can heat, move, or start a job is a
  physical-safety operation, not just a configuration change. The agent never triggers one, and any
  approved change that could cause motion or heating (firmware updates, restarts of the firmware or host
  with a job queued, power-device changes, config changes that take effect on restart) needs the user
  **present at the printer**, with the bed clear, able to cut power.
- **Assume the printer will do what it is told.** Printers act on G-code with few checks. Firmware limits
  (maximum temperatures, thermal-runaway detection, soft endstops) are the only guard, and on Klipper
  those limits live in a text configuration file that the web interface can edit.
- **The host software is a shell on a Linux computer.** OctoPrint plugins are Python code that runs inside
  the OctoPrint server with its rights. Moonraker can install and update software from git repositories,
  run system commands through its machine component, and edit Klipper's configuration. An OctoPrint or
  Moonraker admin is effectively an admin of the host.
- **Vendors say: never port-forward.** OctoPrint's maintainer, Mainsail's documentation, and Prusa's
  PrusaLink documentation all tell users not to open the printer or its host to the internet with a
  router port forward, and to use a VPN or a vetted remote-access service instead.
- **Read-only means read-only.** The agent must never start, pause, resume, or cancel prints, send G-code
  or console commands, change temperatures or fans, home or move axes, upload, rename, or delete files,
  update firmware, toggle power devices, or publish to a printer's MQTT topics. "Just a quick test" of a
  control path is forbidden: it heats or moves a machine nobody is watching.
- **Access codes, API keys, and stream URLs are secrets.** A Bambu access code, an OctoPrint or Moonraker
  API key, a Prusa Connect or PrusaLink credential, or a camera URL with a token gives control or a view of
  the room. Never print, paste, or store them in a report; confirm they exist and where they're stored.
- **Vendor cloud changes behavior without notice.** Bambu Lab's 2025 authorization firmware changed what
  third-party tools can do, and Developer Mode reopened it on an opt-in basis. Check current vendor
  documentation for the exact model and firmware before stating what a mode allows.

## Deployment variants

| Variant | How to recognize it | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bambu Lab, cloud mode** (default) | Printer bound to a Bambu account; used from Bambu Studio or Bambu Handy remotely. | The Bambu account (password, MFA, linked devices, shared printers) controls the printer from anywhere. Needs internet egress. Print history and remote video go through the cloud. |
| **Bambu Lab, LAN Only mode** | Printer setting "LAN Only" on; access code shown on the printer's network screen. | No cloud connection; control from Bambu Studio or Bambu Connect on the LAN. On firmware with the authorization control system, LAN control still requires the vendor's authorization. Handy app, remote printing, and cloud print history stop. |
| **Bambu Lab, LAN Only + Developer Mode** | Developer Mode enabled on the printer after LAN Only (with a risk notice the user accepted). | Bambu documents that this opens the MQTT channel, live stream, and FTP for full control by third-party software, unsupported by Bambu. The access code is then effectively the only credential: anyone on the LAN who has it can control the printer. |
| **Bambu Lab, older firmware** (before the authorization system) | Firmware version below the release that introduced authorization for that model. | Third-party tools keep full LAN control, but the printer misses later security fixes. Bambu says users can stay on old firmware; that trade-off is a finding to document, not to hide. |
| **Prusa with PrusaLink / Prusa Connect** | PrusaLink web UI on the printer (built in on xBuddy printers such as MK4/S, CORE One, XL, MINI+ with Wi-Fi; on a Raspberry Pi for MK3/S/+ and MK2.5/S). Prusa Connect is Prusa's cloud. | PrusaLink is local; Prusa says not to port-forward it. Prusa Connect control is tied to the Prusa account. A Pi-based PrusaLink brings in a separate Linux host. |
| **Klipper on a separate computer** (Raspberry Pi or similar) with Moonraker and Mainsail or Fluidd | Mainsail or Fluidd web UI; Moonraker API on 7125; a microcontroller board in the printer runs Klipper's MCU firmware. | Moonraker's `[authorization]` section is the access-control layer; Mainsail/Fluidd have none of their own. The Pi is a full Linux host. |
| **Klipper built into the printer** (for example Creality K1-series and similar) | Vendor app plus a Fluidd/Mainsail UI on a non-standard port (commonly reported as 4408/4409 on Creality K1-series); vendor "root" option on the screen. | Vendor firmware, vendor cloud, and an embedded Linux system. Enabling root (an on-screen vendor option) gives SSH with a vendor-shown password; treat a rooted printer as a Linux host with whatever the community scripts installed. |
| **OctoPrint** (often the OctoPi image on a Raspberry Pi) attached by USB | OctoPrint web UI; printer connected over USB serial. | OctoPrint access control, API keys, and plugins are the control plane. A separate webcam streamer may serve video outside OctoPrint's login. |
| **Third-party print managers and remote-access services** (for example Obico, OctoEverywhere, SimplyPrint, self-hosted Bambu-aware managers) | Plugin, agent, or container linked to an external account. | A second control plane with its own account, tokens, and vulnerabilities. Self-hosted managers have had critical flaws (for example a 2026 advisory for a self-hosted Bambu management tool with a hard-coded signing key and unauthenticated API routes). |

## Detection

Hints for recognizing this product during a network inventory (used by the `full-assessment` skill).
Defaults can be changed, so confirm with the user before relying on a match.

- **OctoPrint:** web UI titled "OctoPrint" on TCP 5000 by default; on the OctoPi image it is usually
  fronted by a reverse proxy on 80/443. The bundled discovery plugin announces `_octoprint._tcp` and
  `_http._tcp` over mDNS/DNS-SD, and can announce over SSDP for Windows network discovery.
- **Moonraker:** HTTP and WebSocket API on TCP 7125 by default (binds to all IPv4 interfaces unless
  configured otherwise); `GET /server/info` answers with Moonraker JSON (an authorization error for
  untrusted clients, full state for trusted ones). Its optional `[zeroconf]` component announces over
  mDNS, and over SSDP if `enable_ssdp` is set.
- **Mainsail / Fluidd:** static web front ends on 80 (or 4408/4409 on Creality K1-series, as commonly
  reported) with page titles "Mainsail" or "Fluidd"; they talk to Moonraker on 7125 or through the same
  web server.
- **Bambu Lab:** SSDP-style announcements on UDP 2021 (and 1990, per Bambu's port table) used for
  device discovery in cloud and LAN mode; MQTT over TLS on TCP 8883, implicit FTPS on TCP 990 (passive
  data ports 50000–50100), and LAN live video on TCP 6000 (and 322 on models with RTSP live view), per
  Bambu's printer network ports page. Steady TLS connections to Bambu cloud endpoints in cloud mode.
- **PrusaLink:** a PrusaLink-branded web UI on port 80 of the printer (or of its Raspberry Pi); the HTTP
  API asks for digest authentication. Outbound connections to Prusa Connect when linked.
- **MAC vendors (OUI):** Raspberry Pi hosts usually show a Raspberry Pi vendor. Printers with built-in
  Wi-Fi often show the Wi-Fi module's maker rather than the printer brand, so a match on the brand is not
  expected.
- **Behavior:** printers idle most of the time and then exchange status every second or so with a slicer,
  phone app, or cloud during a job; cameras stream continuously when a viewer is open.

## Discover

All operations in this mode are class **R** (read-only). Confirm scope and access first (core: operating
principles). Mark anything you can't inspect **Not assessed**.

### Baseline commands

Prefer sources that don't touch the printer: the router or firewall's DHCP leases, ARP and UPnP tables,
port-forward list and firewall logs; the slicer's and app's device lists (the user reads them out);
screenshots the user takes of printer settings screens; and host-side files read on the Raspberry Pi with
the user's agreement. Candidate checks, each **not yet verified** on every version and install:

```sh
# Light TCP connect check of known printer ports on one host (no OS/version detection, no UDP sweep):
nmap -sT -Pn --max-retries 1 --scan-delay 200ms -p 22,80,443,322,990,4408,4409,5000,6000,7125,8080,8883 <printer-ip>
curl -sI http://<printer-ip>/                     # which UI answers; does it redirect to HTTPS?
curl -s  http://<host-ip>:7125/server/info        # Moonraker: does it answer without credentials?
                                                  # (an answer with full data suggests a trusted client or no auth)
curl -sI http://<host-ip>:5000/                   # OctoPrint: is the UI reachable directly, bypassing a proxy?
```

On a Klipper or OctoPrint host, with shell access the user grants (read only; labeled per source):

```sh
# Moonraker/Klipper (default data folder layout; paths may differ per install; not yet verified everywhere)
sed -n '/^\[authorization\]/,/^\[/p' ~/printer_data/config/moonraker.conf   # trusted_clients, cors, force_logins
grep -nE '^\[(update_manager|mqtt|power|machine|zeroconf|octoprint_compat|webcam)' ~/printer_data/config/moonraker.conf
grep -nE '^\[(verify_heater|extruder|heater_bed|gcode_shell_command)' ~/printer_data/config/*.cfg
grep -nE 'max_temp|min_temp|max_error|check_gain_time' ~/printer_data/config/printer.cfg
ls -l ~/printer_data/logs/                        # moonraker.log, klippy.log (names and dates)
# OctoPrint (default base folder; OctoPi uses the same layout; not yet verified everywhere)
ls ~/.octoprint/plugins/; ~/oprint/bin/pip list 2>/dev/null | grep -i octoprint   # installed plugins
grep -nE 'accessControl|autologin|localNetworks|trustBasicAuthentication|trustRemoteUser' ~/.octoprint/config.yaml
grep -nE '^ *(events|system|scripts):' ~/.octoprint/config.yaml                   # command hooks
ls -l ~/.octoprint/logs/
```

- Read `config.yaml`, `moonraker.conf`, and `moonraker.secrets` **only in the sections you need**. They
  hold API keys, password hashes, MQTT and Home Assistant tokens, and notifier URLs. Never print a whole
  file or a secrets file; report that a secret exists, not its value.
- Read printer settings through the vendor screen, app, or web UI with the user logged in, or from
  screenshots. Prefer that over any API.
- **Never:** start, pause, resume, or cancel a print; send G-code, console, or macro commands (including
  `M112`, `FIRMWARE_RESTART`, `SAVE_CONFIG`); change temperatures, fans, lights, or speeds; home or move
  axes; upload, rename, or delete files (including via FTPS); trigger firmware updates; toggle Moonraker
  or OctoPrint power devices; publish to the printer's MQTT topics or Moonraker's MQTT API topic; connect
  to Bambu MQTT or FTPS with the access code; try default, setup-sticker, or guessed passwords; run
  brute-force tools, exploit or proof-of-concept scripts, or vulnerability-scanner plugins; enable root,
  SSH, or Developer Mode to "look around"; or factory-reset anything.
- If a check leaves a printer or host unresponsive, stop all checks on it and tell the user; an
  interrupted job may need attention at the printer.

### Assessment domains

Every domain must end with a status in the report (Pass / Finding / Not assessed / Not applicable /
Accepted risk).

#### A. Physical safety and fire protection

- Is anyone normally present when the printer runs? Does the user print overnight or while away?
- Smoke detector in the room; printer on a non-flammable surface; nothing flammable on or around it;
  enclosure fans and filters as the vendor intends. These are the controls that matter if everything else
  fails; record them even though they're not network settings.
- **Thermal-runaway protection** in place on every heater. Stock firmware from Bambu, Prusa, and Creality
  ships it. On Klipper, check that no `[verify_heater]` section loosens the defaults far beyond what the
  Klipper documentation suggests, and that `max_temp` on the extruder and bed is a realistic value for the
  hardware (these are the firmware's safety checks). On Marlin-based firmware the user built themselves,
  ask whether thermal protection was compiled in.
- **Who can change those limits remotely:** on Klipper, Mainsail and Fluidd can edit `printer.cfg`
  through Moonraker's file manager, so anyone with Moonraker access can change heater limits and restart
  the firmware. Treat Moonraker access as fire-risk access.
- **Remote start safeguards:** does the platform require someone at the printer to confirm the bed is
  clear before a remote job starts? (Prusa Connect uses a "ready" state set at the printer; check the
  current behavior for each platform.) Do Moonraker job queues or power devices start jobs or power on
  the printer automatically (`queue_gcode_uploads`, `load_on_startup`, `on_when_job_queued`)?
- **Power control:** smart plugs or Moonraker/OctoPrint power devices that can power the printer on
  remotely; who can use them; whether `locked_while_printing` (Moonraker) is set so power can't be cut
  mid-job by mistake.

#### B. Internet exposure and remote access

- Router or firewall port forwards, DMZ host, or UPnP mappings that point at the printer or its host.
  Any internet reachability of OctoPrint, Moonraker, Mainsail/Fluidd, PrusaLink, or Bambu LAN ports is
  **P1** by default (the vendors say never to do this), and **P0 triage** if logs show unknown use.
- Reverse proxies or tunnels (for example a cloud tunnel or a web server on the Pi) that publish the UI:
  what authentication sits in front, and does the backend see the proxy's address as a trusted local
  client (Moonraker `trusted_clients` containing `127.0.0.1`, or OctoPrint autologin for localhost)?
  That combination gives the internet trusted access.
- IPv6: does the printer or host have a global IPv6 address that the firewall allows inbound?
- How the user actually reaches the printer from outside: VPN to home (preferred), vendor cloud (Bambu
  cloud, Prusa Connect, Creality cloud), or a third-party service (Obico, OctoEverywhere, SimplyPrint). Each
  service is an account that can control the printer; list them all.
- Third-party remote-access plugins and agents: maintained? Linked to which account? Still used?

#### C. OctoPrint access control, API keys, and plugins

- Version and update channel; compare with OctoPrint's release notes and GitHub security advisories.
  OctoPrint has published several advisories since 2024 involving upload endpoints, file names,
  cross-site scripting, and API key handling, so being behind matters.
- Access control: mandatory since 1.5.0 (it can no longer be turned off). Check the user list, who is
  in the Admins group, and the permissions given to the Users and Guests groups. Guests (anonymous
  users) get nothing by default, and OctoPrint advises against granting them anything without a VPN;
  anonymous read access to files, webcam, or terminal is a finding.
- **Autologin:** if enabled, `localNetworks` must be narrow (a single admin host, not a whole LAN, and
  never `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0`). An autologin-related authentication bypass was fixed in 2024; if autologin
  sits behind a reverse proxy, the proxy must pass the real client address correctly.
- `trustBasicAuthentication` / `trustRemoteUser` (accepting identity from a reverse proxy): only with a
  proxy that strips and sets those headers itself.
- API keys: per-user keys and application keys (granted through the app-key workflow); a global API key
  on older installs. Which exist, who owns them, whether each is still needed. A key has its owner's
  permissions.
- **Plugins as arbitrary code:** list every third-party plugin, its source, maintainer, last release,
  and whether it's still used. Plugins run inside the OctoPrint server with its rights, can add API
  endpoints, and can read the configuration. Abandoned plugins are a finding. Plugins installed from a URL
  or archive (not the official repository) need extra scrutiny.
- **Command hooks:** `events` subscriptions and `system` actions in `config.yaml` that run shell
  commands, and G-code scripts in Settings (OctoPrint warns against pasting G-code scripts from untrusted
  sources; a 2023 advisory showed an admin-configured script could run code on the host).
- Safe mode (starts without third-party plugins) is a vendor-documented troubleshooting step the user
  can run; it is not part of Discover.

#### D. Moonraker, Klipper, Mainsail, and Fluidd

- `[authorization]`: `trusted_clients` (trusted clients get **full API access**, no login). Installer
  defaults often list every private address range; that trusts every device on the LAN, including IoT
  and guest devices. Prefer an admin subnet or specific hosts, or users with `force_logins: True`.
- Users configured? `force_logins` (requires login once a user exists, overriding trusted clients),
  `max_login_attempts`, `login_timeout`. `default_source` (Moonraker or LDAP); LDAP setups need a current
  Moonraker (an LDAP filter-injection issue was fixed in 2026).
- `cors_domains`: no `*` (Moonraker's docs reserve the wildcard for client developers, not production).
- `[server]`: `host` (defaults to all IPv4 interfaces); `use_xheaders` only behind a proxy, because it
  makes Moonraker trust `X-Forwarded-For`/`X-Real-IP` for the client address (spoofable when reached
  directly).
- API key (enabled by default): who has it, where it's stored (slicers, Home Assistant, phone apps,
  remote-access agents). Regenerate it if it has been widely shared.
- `[update_manager]`: every `git_repo` and `web` entry is software Moonraker will fetch and update on the
  host. Each must be a source the user recognizes; Moonraker warns that third-party extensions need care.
- `[machine]` `sudo_password` set? If so, it must come from the secrets file, and it means Moonraker can
  run privileged commands.
- `[mqtt]`: broker, credentials (from `moonraker.secrets`), TLS, and whether the MQTT API (requests
  accepted over MQTT) is enabled. If it is, anyone who can publish to that topic on the broker can call the
  Moonraker API; check the broker's ACLs with the [MQTT skill](../mqtt/SKILL.md).
- `[octoprint_compat]`: an OctoPrint-style upload API for slicers; note it's another way in.
- `[power]` devices and their credentials (smart-plug, Home Assistant, or MQTT tokens) and
  `locked_while_printing`.
- `moonraker.secrets`: exists, readable only by the service user, not inside a folder Moonraker serves.
- Klipper extras outside upstream Klipper that run shell commands from G-code (for example a
  `[gcode_shell_command]` section added by an installer script): any macro can then run commands on the
  host. List those macros.
- Creality K1-series and similar: whether root was enabled on the screen, whether the vendor-shown root
  password was changed, what community scripts were installed, and whether SSH is reachable from beyond
  an admin host.

#### E. Bambu Lab accounts, modes, access codes, and LAN interfaces

- Mode per printer: cloud, LAN Only, or LAN Only + Developer Mode; firmware version per model; whether
  the firmware includes the authorization control system (introduced first on the X1 series in a
  January 2025 firmware release, then on other series; check Bambu's release notes for the model).
- **Bambu account:** strong unique password; multifactor authentication on (Bambu documents an
  authenticator-app 2-step verification and an email verification code under some conditions); devices
  and sessions logged in; printers shared with other accounts; MakerWorld and Handy apps on old phones.
- **Access code:** shown on the printer's network screen; it is the LAN credential for MQTT, FTPS, and
  video. Who knows it, where it's stored (slicers, Home Assistant, Bambu-aware managers, scripts), and
  whether the printer offers a way to regenerate it on the installed firmware (verify). In Developer
  Mode, treat it as the only lock on the printer.
- **Developer Mode:** enabled? Why? Bambu states it opens the MQTT channel, live stream, and FTP and is not
  supported. If it's enabled only for status monitoring, note that status reading through MQTT push
  remained available without it per Bambu's announcement.
- LAN interfaces reachable from which segments: 8883 (MQTT), 990 + 50000–50100 (FTPS), 6000/322 (video).
  Only the slicer host and integrations that need them should reach them.
- Integrations: Home Assistant Bambu integrations, Bambu Connect, third-party slicers, and self-hosted
  managers (check each manager's advisories and version; at least one had a critical authentication flaw
  in 2026).

#### F. Prusa (PrusaLink and Prusa Connect)

- Firmware version per printer, compared with Prusa's release notes (Prusa notes older xBuddy firmware
  can't connect to Prusa Connect).
- PrusaLink authentication: HTTP digest (Prusa's default and recommendation) rather than the older API
  key mode where the printer offers the choice; Prusa notes the key is sent unencrypted. Credentials set
  on the printer and not shared widely.
- PrusaLink exposure: local network only (Prusa: "not recommended" to reach it through a router port
  forward; use an encrypted VPN).
- Prusa Connect: Prusa account password and two-factor authentication if offered (verify current
  options); team members and shared printers; printers still linked after a sale; camera tokens.
- Pi-based PrusaLink (MK3/S/+, MK2.5/S): the Pi is a separate Linux host (domain J).

#### G. Cameras

- Built-in cameras (Bambu, Prusa Connect cameras, Creality) and add-on webcams on the host.
- Who can view: OctoPrint's webcam permission vs. a streamer (for example mjpg-streamer, ustreamer, or
  crowsnest) served by a separate process or proxy path that may **not** be covered by OctoPrint's or
  Moonraker's login. Check whether the stream URL loads from another LAN host without credentials (a
  read-only page load, with the user's agreement).
- Bambu LAN video (6000/322): reachable from which segments; Bambu cloud remote video: tied to the
  account.
- What the camera sees: the printer, or also a room where people live or work. Privacy follows the
  [IP cameras skill](../ip-cameras/SKILL.md) (domain H there).
- Timelapses and snapshots: stored where, kept how long, uploaded to which cloud or notifier.

#### H. Firmware, updates, and signing

- Update path per platform: Bambu (cloud or Bambu Studio, plus a documented offline SD-card method),
  Prusa (signed firmware; PrusaSlicer or USB), Creality (vendor OTA), Klipper (MCU firmware the user
  compiles and flashes; no signing), OctoPrint (Software Update plugin from GitHub releases), Moonraker
  update manager.
- **Signing:** Prusa's MK4-family and CORE One printers accept only Prusa-signed firmware in factory
  state; breaking the board's "appendix" allows custom firmware, and Prusa then disclaims liability for
  damage including fire. A broken appendix is a decision to record, not a finding by itself.
- Firmware currency: compare with the vendor's release notes for that exact model. Note deliberate
  holds (for example a Bambu printer kept on pre-authorization firmware for third-party control) as an
  accepted risk with the trade-off spelled out.
- Downloads only from vendor sites or official repositories; checksums checked where published.

#### I. G-code and model files as an input

- Where print files come from: own slicer, model libraries (Printables, MakerWorld, Thingiverse),
  pre-sliced files from others, shared network folders, email.
- **Pre-sliced G-code and project files are code for the printer.** They can set any temperature the
  firmware allows, disable soft endstops, change and save persistent settings (on Marlin, `M500` after
  changed values), call Klipper macros (including any that run shell commands), or trigger host actions
  (OctoPrint `@` commands handled by plugins). Project files (`.3mf`) can carry printer profiles with
  custom start and end G-code. Ask whether files from others are re-sliced locally.
- Who can upload files: OctoPrint and Moonraker users, Bambu FTPS (access code), Prusa Connect members,
  slicer upload keys, network shares mounted on the host.
- File names and upload endpoints have been the source of OctoPrint advisories; keep the host current.

#### J. Raspberry Pi or Linux host

- Assess the host with the [Linux skill](../linux/SKILL.md): OS support status,
  updates, SSH (keys only; no default or shared accounts, which current Raspberry Pi OS images no longer
  create), sudo rules for the print-server user, other services on the host, and backups of the SD card or
  configuration.
- Printer-specific points: the print-server user's group memberships (serial, video, GPIO), passwordless
  sudo granted by installers, and whether the host also runs unrelated services that widen exposure.

#### K. Network placement and egress

- Printer and host on an IoT or maker segment, not on the main user LAN; Wi-Fi on an IoT SSID with WPA2
  or WPA3.
- Rules: only the admin and slicer hosts reach the UI and API ports; the printer and host can't reach
  servers, NAS shares (unless a file share is needed, read-only), or other segments' admin interfaces.
- Egress: LAN-only printers and Klipper or OctoPrint hosts that don't use cloud services can have
  internet access blocked or limited to updates and NTP. Cloud-mode Bambu, Prusa Connect, and remote-access
  plugins need specific egress; list it.
- Discovery across segments: Bambu SSDP and mDNS don't cross VLANs by default; slicers can add printers
  by address instead of opening multicast relays broadly.
- Stable addresses (DHCP reservations) so rules, slicers, and integrations keep pointing at the right
  device.

#### L. Logs and print history

- OctoPrint logs (`octoprint.log`, `serial.log` if enabled, plugin manager log) and its print history;
  Moonraker and Klipper logs (`moonraker.log`, `klippy.log`) and Moonraker's job history database; Bambu
  cloud print history (cloud mode only); Prusa Connect job history.
- Retention, and whether logs leave the host (syslog or a log collector) so a compromised host can't
  erase them.
- Login records: OctoPrint and Moonraker log logins and failed logins; check whether failures are
  visible and whether `max_login_attempts` is set.
- Print history is also a privacy record (what was made, when); note where it's stored.

---

## Recommend

No changes are made in this mode. For each finding, produce a recommendation using the core finding
template, including **Dependencies / blast radius** and the **operation class**.

### Dependency and blast-radius check (required)

List what depends on the setting before recommending a change:

- **Slicers and apps:** Bambu Studio, Bambu Connect, Bambu Handy, OrcaSlicer, PrusaSlicer, Cura, and
  phone apps that send jobs or watch status, and which credential each uses.
- **Integrations:** Home Assistant (Bambu, PrusaLink, Moonraker, OctoPrint integrations), MQTT brokers,
  notifiers (Telegram, Discord, email), power devices, and print farms or managers.
- **Remote access:** VPN, vendor cloud, and third-party services the user relies on to watch long
  prints.
- **Firmware holds:** third-party control that stops working after a Bambu firmware update.
- **Running jobs:** never apply a change that restarts the host, firmware, or printer during a print.
- **Firewall rules and aliases** that match printer and host addresses.

### Recommendation guidance

| Area | Typical recommendation | Consequences to explain |
|---|---|---|
| UI or API reachable from the internet (port forward, DMZ, UPnP, open proxy) | Remove it; use a VPN or a vetted remote-access service. | Remote viewing stops until the VPN or service works; test it first. |
| Reverse proxy makes internet clients look local | Remove `127.0.0.1`/localhost from `trusted_clients` or OctoPrint autologin; require login at the proxy and the backend. | Local tools that relied on trust need credentials or API keys. |
| Moonraker trusts all private ranges | Narrow `trusted_clients` to an admin host or subnet; create users and set `force_logins: True`. | Every client outside the list must log in or use the API key; slicer upload settings change. |
| No Moonraker users / no login | Create a user, enable `force_logins`, set `max_login_attempts`. | Front ends prompt for login; integrations need the API key. |
| Wildcard CORS or `use_xheaders` without a proxy | Remove the wildcard; disable `use_xheaders` unless behind a proxy that sets the header. | Front ends served from other origins must be listed explicitly. |
| Unknown `update_manager` repos, third-party OctoPrint plugins | Remove what isn't recognized or used; keep a list of approved sources. | Features those extensions provided disappear. |
| Shell-command G-code extensions | Remove them, or limit to specific reviewed commands. | Macros that used them stop working. |
| OctoPrint autologin with broad `localNetworks` | Disable, or limit to one admin host. | Users on other devices must log in. |
| Guests can read files, webcam, or terminal | Remove anonymous permissions. | Casual viewing needs an account. |
| Stale OctoPrint/Moonraker API keys | Revoke unused keys; regenerate a widely shared Moonraker key. | Every tool using a revoked key breaks until updated. |
| Bambu Developer Mode on without need | Turn it off (status via MQTT push remains on authorized firmware). | Third-party control (Home Assistant control, some managers) stops. |
| Bambu Developer Mode needed | Keep it, but isolate the printer so only named hosts reach 8883/990/6000; protect the access code like a password. | Narrower access from phones and other hosts. |
| Bambu account without MFA, or shared widely | Enable 2-step verification; review shared printers and logged-in devices. | Each user needs their own account and an authenticator. |
| PrusaLink in API-key mode or credentials shared | Use digest authentication; set new credentials. | Integrations must be updated. |
| Camera stream outside the login | Put the stream behind the same authentication or restrict it to admin hosts; disable unused cameras. | Some apps that pull the raw stream need credentials. |
| Loosened thermal limits on Klipper | Restore vendor or Klipper-documented values with the user present (see Remediate). | None for normal printing; tuning experiments need a documented reason. |
| Untrusted pre-sliced files | Re-slice from the model locally with the user's own profiles. | Extra time; some designer-tuned settings are lost. |
| Flat network or unrestricted egress | Move printers and hosts to an IoT/maker segment; block egress except what each needs. | Cloud features and auto-updates may stop; discovery needs manual addresses. |
| Outdated firmware or host software | Update following vendor instructions, with the user at the printer and no job running. | Restart; Bambu updates may remove third-party control; read release notes. |
| Unsupported host OS on the Pi | Follow the Linux skill; rebuild on a supported image. | Reinstall time; restore configuration from backup. |

Changing default ports and hiding discovery are supplementary only. Never recommend them as the main fix.

Group the plan: immediate containment (if any) → urgent fixes (internet exposure, trusted-proxy bypasses,
unknown extensions) → high-priority hardening (authentication, trusted clients, Developer Mode, account
MFA, segmentation) → routine maintenance (updates, logs) → optional defense in depth. Then ask for
approval (core: modes and authorization).

---

## Remediate

Apply only approved changes, one at a time, following the core rules. 3D-printer specifics:

- **Physical-safety rule.** Any change that could start motion or heating, or that restarts something
  which could, is at least **C2** and needs the user **at the printer**, bed clear, no job running, able
  to cut power. This includes firmware updates, `FIRMWARE_RESTART` or Klipper/Moonraker restarts,
  OctoPrint restarts with a connected printer, edits to heater, endstop, or macro configuration, job-queue
  and power-device changes, and turning Developer Mode or LAN Only on or off. The agent never issues
  motion, heating, print-control, or G-code commands, even when asked to "test" a fix; the user does any
  functional test at the printer.
- **Before any change:** back up the configuration (Moonraker config folder; OctoPrint's built-in Backup &
  Restore, which contains secrets and stays with the user) and record current settings or screenshots.
- **Authentication changes (C2):** add users or keys first, confirm they work from each slicer and
  integration, then narrow `trusted_clients`, enable `force_logins`, or remove autologin. Keep one
  logged-in session open until the new path is verified.
- **Exposure changes (C2):** remove port forwards or proxy routes only after the replacement remote path
  (VPN or service) works for the user.
- **Extensions:** remove plugins or update-manager entries one at a time; restart only with the user
  present; verify the printer UI and connection afterward.
- **Credentials:** the user generates new API keys, passwords, and Bambu access codes (where the firmware
  allows) and updates every consumer. Never paste new secrets into the report.
- **Firmware and software updates:** the user downloads only from the vendor or official repository,
  reads the release notes (Bambu authorization changes, Prusa signing, Klipper MCU compatibility), and
  applies them at the printer. Klipper MCU firmware must match the host version; flashing is a hard stop
  for the agent.
- **Thermal limits:** restore safe values only from the vendor's or Klipper's documented configuration
  for that hardware, with the user present, and have the user watch the first heat-up.

After each change, follow the core "after a change" steps: re-read the setting, confirm from an
untrusted client that access is now refused (a read-only request), confirm slicers and integrations
still connect, and record before and after. Functional printing tests are done by the user.

### Hard stops (refer to a specialist or do manually; never automate)

- Sending G-code, starting or cancelling prints, heating, moving axes, or toggling power, for any reason.
- Disabling or loosening thermal-runaway protection, `min_temp`/`max_temp`, or endstops.
- Flashing printer, MCU, or bootloader firmware; breaking firmware signing; enabling root or SSH on
  vendor firmware.
- Testing default or guessed credentials, connecting with a found access code, brute force, or running
  exploit code.
- Factory resets, and deleting print history, timelapses, or logs.
- Running unreviewed install or "helper" scripts on the host as remediation.

---

## Respond

On any P0 indicator, switch to Respond immediately. Follow the core playbook plus the 3D-printer-specific
steps in [incident-response.md](incident-response.md). If a printer is heating, moving, or printing
without the user's intent, physical safety outranks evidence: the user goes to the printer and stops it
(screen stop, emergency stop, or power off) first.

---

## Worked example (invented)

### P3D-001: Moonraker reachable from the internet as a trusted client through a reverse proxy

**Confidence:** Confirmed
**Priority:** P1. Anyone on the internet gets full, unauthenticated Moonraker access: they can start jobs,
set heater temperatures, and edit `printer.cfg` (including heater limits) on a printer that runs
unattended overnight.
**State:** Open
**Component:** Klipper host (single-board computer) running Moonraker and Mainsail behind a web server on
the same host
**Evidence:** Observed 2026-05-12: the router forwards TCP 443 to the host at `192.0.2.40`. The web server
proxies `/` to Mainsail and `/websocket` and `/server` to `127.0.0.1:7125`. `moonraker.conf` lists
`127.0.0.1` in `trusted_clients`, has no users, and `force_logins` is unset. With approval, a read-only
`GET /server/info` from an outside test host at `198.51.100.23` to `https://printer.example.com/` returned
full Moonraker data without credentials. No other requests were sent.
**Expected secure state:** not reachable from the internet (Mainsail docs: don't open Mainsail/Moonraker
ports to the world); remote access through a VPN; Moonraker requires login for anything but named admin
hosts.
**Exposure and prerequisites:** anyone who finds the host name or address; no credentials needed.
**Dependencies / blast radius:** the user watches long prints remotely through this address; a phone
app and a notifier bot use it. A WireGuard VPN on the firewall exists but isn't set up on the phone.
**Recommended remediation:** (1) set up the VPN on the phone and confirm Mainsail loads over it;
(2) remove the port forward; (3) create a Moonraker user, set `force_logins: True`, and remove
`127.0.0.1` from `trusted_clients`; (4) update the phone app and bot to use the API key.
**Operation class:** C2 (port forward; authentication change; Moonraker restart with the user at the
printer and no job running).
**Approval required:** Yes.
**Verification:** the outside test host gets no response; an unauthenticated `GET /server/info` from
a non-admin LAN host is refused (401); Mainsail over the VPN prompts for login; the user confirms the
printer is idle and normal after the restart.
**Rollback:** restore the saved `moonraker.conf` and router setting (not recommended; fix the VPN instead).
